newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Regional summit ponders Aral Sea eco-disaster.
newsitem.headline: Regional summit ponders Aral Sea eco-disaster.

text.p: The leaders of five Central Asian states gathered in the Kazakh capital on Friday to look for possible solutions to an ecological disaster in the region caused by the vanishing Aral Sea.

The presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan met early in the afternoon in the presidential palace in the centre of Almaty and were later expected to meet officials from the World Bank and the United Nations.
Regional summits here are rare and Friday's meeting underlines the scale of the environmental catastrophe caused by the disappearing inland sea.
The Aral -- once the world's fourth largest lake -- has shrunk since the 1960s from 69,000 square km to about 30,000 square km. Its volume has fallen by three quarters.

The catastrophe was caused by a Soviet-era decision to divert water from two mighty rivers supplying the sea with water -- the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya -- to irrigate marginal land to boost the region's production of cotton.

The supply of water to the sea has reduced to five cubic km a year from about 60 cubic km in the 1960s. Scientists say 35 cubic km of water are needed annually to stop the shrinking of the sea, which straddles Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

Salt dust from the bed of the dying sea, laden with hazardous fertilisers washed down from the cotton fields up-river, are responsible for alarmingly high rates of anaemia, cancer and respiratory diseases among the 3.5 million population living around the sea.
Ports, once centres of a flourishing fishing industry, have been turned into virtual ghost towns in the poisonous desert wastes.
However, demand for water in Central Asia is as high as ever.

Production of the "white gold", or cotton, remains crucial for the hard-hit economies of Central Asia. Water is also needed to fulfil Soviet-style plans by Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, largely desert nations, to be self-sufficient in grain.
The World Bank has granted $41 million to a special intergovernmental fund on the Aral Sea set up by the five states. But hundreds of millions of dollars are needed to tackle the disaster.
